about: WorldScrawl prompts. Edit them in the map window: Tools > Prompt Editor. {{name}} is filled in by the game.

groups.title: Writing style
groups.flow: The prompts and lines that shape the actual prose the model writes. Each one says which process uses it (Narration, Breaking through, Expand with AI) and which step it is there. Step 1: Narration lines tell the narrator what just happened (a move, a trip, a door, breaking through, looking around) and how to describe it. Step 2: Breaking through and New room behind a door say how a new room is named and described, and Map changes says how changed places are described. Step 3: Expand with AI writes a place's description or notes in the place form. These are free to edit; prompts whose wording the game reads back stay locked in their own groups.

groups.title: Shared bases
groups.flow: Not a process of its own: the shared base for every question that asks the model to pick one option from a list (which exit to look at, what to do at a closed door, which place a window shows, which door to open or close). Step 1: the game lists the options as short text keys ("- key: meaning") and sends this system prompt with the question. The answer is matched to a key ignoring case, punctuation and extra words; if nothing matches, the question is asked once more. The shared base lines (pick.base_one, pick.base_json, pick.base_text) are the generic reply rules every system prompt ends with; each call's system prompt adds its own task line and fills the base in as {{reply}}. A saved profile that replaced a whole system prompt (without {{reply}}) keeps working as it was.

groups.title: Player intent
groups.flow: Runs on every message the player sends, before the narrator replies. Step 1: one multiple-choice question asks what the player is doing. The game builds the list of choices from the option pieces: one line per exit and per known place, plus 'breaking through', 'look', 'open/close a door' or 'a door not on the map' only when the message uses one of those kinds of words. The answer decides what happens next: an exit or place moves the party; breaking through goes to 'Breaking through'; look goes to 'Looking'; opening or closing a door goes to 'Doors'; a door not on the map tells the narrator to open it if it fits (which can lead to 'New room behind a door'); otherwise the party stays. Step 2 (only if the answer can't be read and no place name matches): a yes/no question asks whether the player is trying to travel at all. Yes means 'somewhere unlisted', no means they stay. Whatever happened is then handed to 'Narration'. Bracket commands: when the message has a known verb in brackets ("I [move] north", "[look] out the window"), step 1 is skipped. The words after the verb are matched to an exit or place by name; only if that fails, 'Bracket command: which target' asks which option they mean. If nothing fits, the game shows a note and the narrator is not called. Unknown bracket words like [OOC: ...] are ignored.

groups.title: Breaking through
groups.flow: Runs when Player intent decides the player is breaking a new opening (a hole in a wall, floor or window). Step 1: one JSON question. The game lists the nearby places (up to 3 steps away) as short keys, plus a new place where new rooms are allowed ("expandable"). The model answers with the place (an existing key, or a new name and description), the opening's name on both sides, and whether the party stays or goes through. The game checks the answer and asks once more, with the error, if it doesn't fit. An existing place just gets the linked pair of exits; a new place is made with the same "create place" edit the editor and New room behind a door use. If it still fails, nothing is changed and the narrator is told nothing gave way. Otherwise the change is saved on the player's message and, unless the answer was "stay", the party moves through. The result is handed to 'Narration'.

groups.title: Looking
groups.flow: Runs when Player intent decides the player is looking or listening. 'Look around' needs no question. Step 1: what are they looking at: around in general, one of the exits, or out of a window (only offered if a window is mentioned or the room has a view). Step 2 depends on the pick: for a closed door, ask whether they listen, peek, open it, or just look at it; for a window with no view set yet, ask which nearby place can be seen (the answer is saved so it's the same next time). The game then works out what can be seen or heard and hands it to 'Narration'.

groups.title: Doors
groups.flow: Runs when Player intent decides the player opens or closes a door. If only one door fits, no question is asked. Step 1 (only with several doors): which door. The game fills {{verb}} with "open" or "close". The game then opens or closes it (or notes it is stuck), saves that on the player's message, and hands it to 'Narration'.

groups.title: Narration
groups.flow: Not a separate model call: this is the block of world facts the game adds to the narrator's own prompt every turn, so the story matches the map. It is put together in order: Step 1 the first line; then the game's own facts (place, exits, what can be seen, time, weather); Step 2 one 'what just happened' line chosen from the result of Player intent, Breaking through, Looking or Doors (a move, a journey, breaking through, a door, a door not on the map, looking around, and so on); Step 3 things passed on the way (after a move); Step 4 a nudge to mention the exits; Step 5 the last line with the rules. Alongside it: the arrival reminder goes after the latest message on move turns, and when map tools are off the two 'how to flag' hints tell the narrator to end a reply with [ws_flag: …] or [ws_wait: …] tags, which start 'Map changes', 'New room behind a door' or a wait. Whether a mentioned room may be flagged as a discovery follows the 'Proactive room discovery' setting (off: only a door actually opened or entered; on: rooms the narration mentions too); the matching off/on pieces fill {{discover}}. When a saved person is in the scene, the people-here block ({{npcs_present}} and {{npc_focus}}) is added with the world facts.

groups.title: People
groups.flow: Runs when a saved person might be part of the turn. Step 1, only when the player's words do not already name one person who is here: a pick-one question asks who they are addressing or looking at (the keys are those people's ids, plus nobody). How deeply that person is described is decided from the words (a look or a talk is focused; a question about their past is deep), not a second question. The first time someone with no starting attitude is met, a separate pick-one assigns one, leaning toward indifferent. Remembering someone is its own JSON question: it reads the story since they showed up and answers with a name and one line. The narrator reports new facts with the ws_npc tool, or with a [ws_npc: …] tag when tools are off.

groups.title: Map changes
groups.flow: Runs when a message is flagged as changing the map: the flag button, the narrator's ws_flag tool or [ws_flag: …] tag, or /ws-change. Step 1: given the story and an outline of the nearby map, the model answers in JSON which places changed. If none, it stops. Step 2: the game sends just those places (plus neighbours and other mentions, via the pieces) and the list of map edits the editor can make; the model answers with JSON edits, or says it can't express it, or that nothing changed. How changed descriptions are written comes from the Writing style entry 'Map changes: how descriptions are written'; the edit format stays locked here. The game test-applies the edits; if they don't fit the map, Step 2 is asked once more with the retry piece explaining the error. The result becomes a review card (or is kept at once if 'keep automatically' is on).

groups.title: New room behind a door
groups.flow: Runs when the narrator opens a door that isn't on the map yet and flags it as a discovery (from the 'door not on the map' narration). Step 1: the model gets the region and area notes, the current room, its exits, nearby rooms and the story, and answers in JSON with the new room and the door pair. If places nearby are not yet connected to this room, they are listed as short keys (the existing piece) and the model may instead answer with one of them; then only the door pair to that place is added. The new room's name and description follow the Writing style entry 'New room behind a door: how it is named and described'. The game turns that into the same 'create place' edit the editor uses and test-applies it; if it doesn't fit, Step 1 is asked once more with the retry piece. The room is added at once, as if it had always been there; its 'Map changed here' bar offers Edit, Turn off and Undo.

groups.title: Expand with AI
groups.flow: Runs when you press 'Expand with AI' under a description or notes box in the map editor. Step 1: one call with the place's region, area and connected places, which box it is (the field pieces), and your draft if the box already has text. The reply is put into the box for you to keep or change; nothing is saved until you save the form.

placeholders.address: the address of the room behind the door
placeholders.area: the address of the area being changed
placeholders.areas: the area notes that apply, for context
placeholders.arrival: what the party sees on arrival (the new room's description)
placeholders.context: what is already around the place (its region, area and neighbours), or empty
placeholders.cut_short: empty, or " (the trip was cut short there)" when the trip stopped early (the Narration piece)
placeholders.description: the description of the room the prompt is about
placeholders.direction: the exit or direction, e.g. "north", "up" or "through the trapdoor"
placeholders.door: the door being used, e.g. "the north door"
placeholders.draft: your draft text for the field, or empty (the Expand with AI piece)
placeholders.edit_types: the list of map edit types the model may use (made by the game)
placeholders.end: where the story text to look at ends
placeholders.error: what was wrong with the last answer
placeholders.existing: nearby places not yet connected to this room, offered as an alternative to a new room (empty when there are none)
placeholders.exits: the list of exits from the current room, one per line, or "- (none)" when there are none
placeholders.field: which text to write: the description or the notes (the Expand with AI pieces)
placeholders.how_to_flag: how the narrator should flag a new door: the tools version or the [ws_flag] tag version (the Narration pieces)
placeholders.kind: what kind of place it is: "region", "area" or "room"
placeholders.label: the name of a place the player already knows about
placeholders.mentions: other world text that names a changed place (from the Map changes piece), or empty
placeholders.name: the name of the place (new or being changed)
placeholders.near: the places near the new room
placeholders.neighbors: the places one step beyond the change (from the Map changes piece), or empty
placeholders.new_place: The new-place option, only where new rooms are allowed (empty otherwise).
placeholders.note: the narrator's note naming the door
placeholders.option: the short answer word for this choice, e.g. "look" or "stay"
placeholders.option_lines: the list of possible answers, one per line, each with what it means (built from the Player intent pieces)
placeholders.options: the possible answers: "- key: meaning" lines (pick-one questions) or a comma-separated list (intent)
placeholders.outline: an outline of the rooms and exits in the area
placeholders.party: who is travelling: the "Who moves" setting, e.g. your persona name, or your persona and the character
placeholders.place: the name of the room the party is in now
placeholders.places: the nearby places, one "- key: name: short summary" line each
placeholders.range: which rooms the patch may touch
placeholders.retry: empty, or a note that the last answer was rejected and why (the retry piece)
placeholders.rooms: the rooms that may be changed, with their current text
placeholders.said: what the player just wrote (their latest message)
placeholders.start: where the story text to look at starts
placeholders.steps: what happened on the way, step by step, joined with "Then:"
placeholders.story: the part of the story that changed the map
placeholders.style: The Writing style entry for this process (how names and descriptions are written), filled in by the game.
placeholders.target: What the player wrote after a bracket command's verb, e.g. "north" in "[move] north".
placeholders.to: the room the party arrived in
placeholders.used: The exit names already used at this place, comma-separated, or "none".
placeholders.verb: the door action: "open" or "close" in the door question; "opens" or "closes" in the narration line
placeholders.via: the rooms passed through on the way, comma separated
placeholders.what: what change was flagged, in the narrator's words
placeholders.where: where the party is now, for the narrator
placeholders.why: why the door would not move (e.g. it is locked)
placeholders.reply: The shared base reply line (pick.base_one, pick.base_json or pick.base_text) that ends this system prompt. Filled in by the game.
placeholders.amount: The wait amount as the player wrote it, e.g. "a bit over an hour".
placeholders.ended: how a temporary change ran out, e.g. "Guest Room 1 expired at 9:00 PM, 3 Mar (lasted 1h, from message #5)"
placeholders.change: the summary of the map change that made the place
placeholders.excerpt: a short excerpt of the chat message that made the place
placeholders.default: the key to use when unsure (the way the party came in)
placeholders.discover: The discovery wording, filled in by the game: the 'Proactive room discovery' off or on piece (the scene can override the setting).
placeholders.npcs_present: The saved people in this scene, one short line each: name, what they are doing, and how they feel about the player.
placeholders.npc_focus: The person the player is addressing, with manner, voice and memory, plus history when the talk goes deep. Empty when nobody is the focus.
placeholders.how_to_report: How the narrator reports a new fact about a person: the ws_npc tool, or the [ws_npc] tag when tools are off.
placeholders.line: One sentence about a person: who they are, as already said in the story or the cast file.

prompts.title: Pick one option: system prompt
prompts.description: Step 1: the system prompt for every pick-one question (Looking and Doors). The options are short text keys. {{reply}} is the shared base line pick.base_one.
prompts.locked: Shared by every pick-one question: the game reads the answer as one option key.
prompts.text: You help run a text adventure game. {{reply}}

prompts.title: Shared base: reply with one option key
prompts.description: Step 1: the shared base line for every pick-one system prompt (pick.system, intent.system). Each call adds its own task line before it.
prompts.locked: The game reads the answer as exactly one option key.
prompts.text: Reply with exactly one option key from the list and nothing else.

prompts.title: Shared base: reply with JSON
prompts.description: Step 1: the shared base line for every JSON system prompt (breaking through, map changes, new rooms). Each call adds its own task line and keys.
prompts.locked: The game parses every JSON answer; the reply must be JSON only.
prompts.text: Reply with JSON only

prompts.title: Shared base: reply with only the text
prompts.description: Step 1: the shared base line for plain-text answers (Expand with AI). The call adds its own task line before it.
prompts.locked: The game puts the whole answer into the field, so it must be the text alone.
prompts.text: Reply with only the text: no title, no quotes, no notes.

prompts.title: Breaking through: system prompt (JSON answer)
prompts.description: Step 1 of 1: the system prompt for the one breaking-through call. It sets the JSON answer: an existing place or a new one, the exit names on both sides, and whether the party goes through. {{reply}} is the shared base line pick.base_json.
prompts.locked: The game reads the JSON answer with these exact keys; changing this can break breaking through.
prompts.text:
You help run a text adventure game. The player is breaking a new opening (a hole in a wall, floor, ceiling or window). {{reply}}:
{"existing": "place key", "direction": "exit name from this side", "return_direction": "exit name from the other side", "then": "stay" or "go_through"}
When a new place is allowed, you may reply {"new": {"name": "...", "description": "..."}} instead of "existing".
direction: one of north, south, east, west, up, down, or a short new word (1-2 words) such as hole, crack, window, breach; never one already used here. return_direction: the way back from the other side (the opposite compass word, or a word like hole); never one the other place already uses. then: "stay" only if the player clearly stays on this side (only making the opening, looking or reaching through); otherwise "go_through".

prompts.title: Breaking through: where it leads and how
prompts.description: Step 1 of 1: the one breaking-through question. The game lists nearby places as keys (and offers a new place only where new rooms are allowed); the model answers in JSON.
prompts.locked: The game reads the JSON answer with these exact keys; changing this can break breaking through.

prompts.title: Breaking through: the new-place option
prompts.description: Piece of the breaking-through question, added only where new rooms are allowed. {{style}} is the Writing style entry for the new room.
prompts.locked: The game reads the JSON answer with these exact keys; changing this can break breaking through.
prompts.text: Or it can lead to a new space nobody has seen yet: then reply "new" instead of "existing". {{style}}

prompts.title: Breaking through: retry
prompts.description: Piece of the breaking-through question, only on the second try: passes the game's error back to the model.
prompts.locked: Part of the JSON retry loop: it passes the game's error back to the model.
prompts.text: Your last answer did not fit: {{error}}. Fix it.

prompts.title: Looking: at what
prompts.description: Step 1 of 2: what the player is looking at. Asks what the player is looking at or listening to. The options (key: meaning) are made by the game.
prompts.locked: The game reads the chosen option key back; changing this can break looking.

prompts.title: Looking: a closed door
prompts.description: Step 2 of 2 (a closed door): listen, peek, open or just look. Asks what the player does with a closed door. The game reads the answer as 1 to 4, in this order.
prompts.locked: The game reads the key: listen, peek, open or look.
prompts.text:
{{said}}

The {{direction}} door is closed. What does the player do with it?
- listen: only listens at it
- peek: peeks through it (a crack, keyhole or gap) without opening it
- open: opens it
- look: just looks at the closed door

Reply with just the key.

prompts.title: Looking: out a window
prompts.description: Step 2 of 2 (a window with no view yet): which nearby place can be seen. Asks which nearby place can be seen out of a window or opening.
prompts.locked: The game reads the chosen place key back; changing this can break looking.

prompts.title: Doors: which door
prompts.description: Step 1 of 1 (only when several doors fit): which door. Asks which door the player opens or closes.
prompts.locked: The game reads the chosen door key back; changing this can break doors.

prompts.title: Player intent: system prompt
prompts.description: Step 1 of 2: the system prompt for the intent question. The system prompt for the question that works out what the player is trying to do. {{reply}} is the shared base line pick.base_one.
prompts.locked: The game reads the answer as exactly one option from the list.
prompts.text: You classify player intent for a text adventure game. {{reply}}

prompts.title: Player intent: the question
prompts.description: Step 1 of 2: the question itself. {{option_lines}} is built from the option pieces below. The multiple-choice question about the player's message. The option lines come from the "Player intent: option" prompts below.
prompts.locked: The game reads the model's answer as one of a fixed set of words; changing this can break how moves are understood.

prompts.title: Player intent option: an exit
prompts.description: Piece: One line per exit.
prompts.locked: The game matches the answer against these option labels.
prompts.text: - {{direction}}: the player goes through the "{{direction}}" exit right now

prompts.title: Player intent option: a known place
prompts.description: Piece: One line per place the player knows about.
prompts.locked: The game matches the answer against these option labels.
prompts.text: - {{label}}: the player travels to {{label}}, a place they know about

prompts.title: Player intent option: breaking through
prompts.description: Piece: Only offered when the player uses a breaking-through word.
prompts.locked: The game matches the answer against these option labels.
prompts.text: - {{option}}: the player clearly breaks through a wall, floor, ceiling or window right now, making a new opening (not just hitting, kicking or touching it)

prompts.title: Player intent option: looking
prompts.description: Piece: Only offered when the player uses a looking word.
prompts.locked: The game matches the answer against these option labels.
prompts.text: - {{option}}: the player looks, peers, peeks or listens at something from here, without going anywhere

prompts.title: Player intent option: opening a door
prompts.description: Piece: Offered only when the message fits.
prompts.locked: The game matches the answer against these option labels.
prompts.text: - {{option}}: the player opens a closed door here, without going through it

prompts.title: Player intent option: closing a door
prompts.description: Piece: Offered only when the message fits.
prompts.locked: The game matches the answer against these option labels.
prompts.text: - {{option}}: the player closes an open door here

prompts.title: Player intent option: a door not on the map
prompts.description: Piece: Offered only when the message fits.
prompts.locked: The game matches the answer against these option labels.
prompts.text: - {{option}}: the player opens or tries a door, hatch or stair that is none of the exits listed above (e.g. another door along a hallway)

prompts.title: Player intent option: staying
prompts.description: Piece: Offered only when the message fits.
prompts.locked: The game matches the answer against these option labels.
prompts.text: - {{option}}: the player is not trying to travel anywhere

prompts.title: Player intent option: somewhere unlisted
prompts.description: Piece: Offered only when the message fits.
prompts.locked: The game matches the answer against these option labels.
prompts.text: - {{option}}: the player wants to go to a place that is not listed above

prompts.description: Piece: Offered only when the message fits.
prompts.locked: The game matches the answer against these option labels.
prompts.text: - {{option}}: the player wants to travel, but it is unclear which of the listed places they mean

prompts.title: Bracket command: which target
prompts.description: Step 1 (bracket commands only): used only when the words after a bracket verb ("I [move] up the stairs") don't name an exit or place exactly. The options (key: meaning) are made by the game.
prompts.locked: The game reads the chosen option key back; changing this can break bracket commands.

prompts.title: Travel check: system prompt
prompts.description: Step 2 of 2 (only if step 1's answer can't be read): the system prompt for the yes/no travel check. For the yes/no follow-up when the intent answer could not be read.
prompts.locked: The game reads the answer as exactly 'yes' or 'no'.
prompts.text: Reply with exactly one word: yes or no.

prompts.title: Travel check: the question
prompts.description: Step 2 of 2 (only if step 1's answer can't be read): asks whether the player is trying to travel. Must be answered yes or no. Asked when the intent answer could not be read. Must be answered yes or no.
prompts.locked: The game reads the model's answer as one of a fixed set of words; changing this can break how moves are understood.

prompts.title: Waits: reading a loose amount
prompts.description: Alongside bracket commands and /ws-wait: used only when a wait amount ([wait], [sleep], /ws-wait or the narrator's wait tag) is not in a form the game reads itself. The game reads the JSON answer.
prompts.locked: The game reads the JSON answer.
prompts.text: You turn a player's description of how long to wait into a number. {{reply}}: {"seconds": N} for an amount of time, {"until": "dawn|morning|noon|dusk|evening|night|midnight|HH:MM"} for a time of day, or {"unknown": true} if it says no amount.

prompts.description: Alongside bracket commands and /ws-wait: the loose wait amount itself.
prompts.locked: The game reads the JSON answer.
prompts.text: How long is this wait? "{{amount}}"

prompts.description: Step 1 of 5: the first line. First line of the world state given to the narrator each turn.
prompts.locked: The narrator relies on this marker to know the block is from the game.
prompts.text: [World state from the game engine. This is authoritative.]

prompts.text: What just happened: {{party}} travelled from {{from}} through {{via}} to {{to}}{{cut_short}}.{{arrival}} Narrate the journey briefly, in that order, ending with arriving in {{where}}.

prompts.text: (the trip was cut short there)

prompts.title: Breaking through: how the new room is named and described
prompts.description: Used by Breaking through. Step 1 (somewhere new only): how the new room's name and description are written. Added to the breaking-through question.
prompts.text: Name it in 2-3 words (like Dusty Crawlspace) and describe it in one short sentence.

prompts.title: Narration: broke through and went
prompts.description: Used by Narration. Step 2 of 5 (one 'what just happened' line is picked): broke through and went.
prompts.text: What just happened: {{party}} broke through, making a new opening ({{direction}}) from {{from}}, and went straight through it.{{arrival}} Narrate breaking through and arriving in {{where}}.

prompts.title: Narration: broke through, stayed
prompts.description: Used by Narration. Step 2 of 5 (one 'what just happened' line is picked): broke through, stayed.
prompts.text: What just happened: {{party}} broke through, making a new opening ({{direction}}) from here to {{to}}. It exists now and is listed in the exits. {{party}} has not gone through it yet and is still at {{place}}. Narrate the breakthrough.

Narrate the attempt failing (the wall, floor or window holds), and do not flag a map change or a new room for it.

prompts.title: Narration: a stuck door
prompts.description: Used by Narration. Step 2 of 5 (one 'what just happened' line is picked): a stuck door.
prompts.text: What just happened: {{party}} tries to open the {{door}}, but it {{why}}. It stays shut. {{party}} stays at {{place}}.

prompts.title: Narration: opening or closing a door
prompts.description: Used by Narration. Step 2 of 5 (one 'what just happened' line is picked): opening or closing a door.
prompts.text: What just happened: {{party}} {{verb}} the {{door}}. {{party}} stays at {{place}}.

prompts.title: Narration: a door not on the map
prompts.description: Used by Narration. Step 2 of 5 (one 'what just happened' line is picked): a door not on the map.
prompts.text: What just happened: {{party}} tries a door that is not among the exits. If such a door plausibly fits {{place}} (its description and the area notes), narrate it opening and {{how_to_flag}}; the engine adds the room behind it. If no such door fits, narrate that there is none. {{party}} stays at {{place}} for now.

prompts.description: Used by Narration. Step 2 of 5 (one 'what just happened' line is picked): looking around.
prompts.text: What just happened: {{party}} looks around {{place}}. {{party}} stays here.

prompts.text: In this reply, mention every exit listed above, and weave in what can be seen through the open ones (the "you can see" lines). For an exit listed without a destination, mention only the exit itself; do not hint or guess where it leads.

prompts.title: Narration: a temporary place ends
prompts.description: Used by Narration. Step 2 of 2 when a temporary place runs out with the party inside (setting "Narrate expiries"): the game has already picked where the party ends up and moved them; this line, sent with one automatic narrator reply, lets the narrator decide why and how the place ends.

prompts.title: Narration: how to flag map changes
prompts.description: Alongside (map tools off, flag tags on): tells the narrator how to tag map changes (permanent or temporary) and door discoveries. The discovery sentence depends on 'Proactive room discovery'.
prompts.locked: The exact [ws_flag: …] tag format the game looks for.
prompts.text: If something in the story changes a place, for good or for a while (it burns down, collapses, floods, fills with smoke, a door is smashed or barricaded, a portal opens for an hour), end your reply with [ws_flag: place | what changed]. {{discover}} Never write it otherwise.

prompts.title: Narration: flagging a discovery (Proactive room discovery off)
prompts.description: Piece: fills {{discover}} in 'how to flag map changes' when Proactive room discovery is off: only a door that is actually opened or entered counts.
prompts.locked: The exact [ws_flag: discover | …] tag the game looks for.
prompts.text: If the characters actually open or go through a door that is not one of the exits, and the room description mentions it or such a door plausibly fits the room, end your reply with [ws_flag: discover | which door]. A door or room that is only mentioned in the scenery (a hallway "lined with four guest rooms") is not a discovery: do not flag it. If no such door fits, there is none: do not flag it.

prompts.title: Narration: flagging a discovery (Proactive room discovery on)
prompts.description: Piece: fills {{discover}} in 'how to flag map changes' when Proactive room discovery is on: rooms the narration mentions may be added too.
prompts.locked: The exact [ws_flag: discover | …] tag the game looks for.
prompts.text: If the characters open or go through a door that is not one of the exits, or your narration names a room or passage off this place that is not on the map yet (e.g. the guest rooms along a hallway), and it fits the room, end your reply with [ws_flag: discover | which door or room]; the engine adds it to the map. If nothing like that fits, do not flag it.

prompts.title: Narration: how to pass time
prompts.description: Alongside (map tools off, flag tags on): tells the narrator when and how to tag time passing in the scene.
prompts.locked: The exact [ws_wait: …] tag format the game looks for.
prompts.text: End your reply with [ws_wait: 2h] (or [ws_wait: 45m], [ws_wait: until dusk], [ws_wait: sleep until morning]) whenever a meaningful amount of time (about 15 minutes or more) passes in the scene without travelling, not just long waits or sleep: a long meal or conversation, searching a room thoroughly, crafting, a lengthy task, resting, sleeping the night, or a time skip. Give your best guess at how long. Do not use it for moment-to-moment action or for travel (moves already count their own time). The player can adjust or discard it, so when in doubt, propose it. Never write it otherwise.

prompts.title: Narration: the ws_wait tool description (tools on)
prompts.description: Alongside (map tools on): the description of the ws_wait tool, telling the narrator when to pass time.
prompts.locked: Names the ws_wait tool's duration and until arguments, which the game reads.
prompts.text: Call this whenever a meaningful amount of time (about 15 minutes or more) passes in the scene without travelling, not just long waits or sleep: a long meal or conversation, searching a room thoroughly, crafting, a lengthy task, resting, sleeping the night, or a time skip. Give your best guess at how long. Do not use it for moment-to-moment action or for travel (moves already count their own time). The player can adjust or discard it, so when in doubt, propose it. Give a duration ("45m", "2h", "1h30m", "2d") or a time to wait until ("morning", "dusk", "14:00"). The game clock moves on once the player keeps it; the result says the new time.

prompts.title: Map changes: how descriptions are written
prompts.description: Used by Map changes (step 2): how changed descriptions are written, the description rule, and people in a room. Added to its system prompt.
prompts.text:
Descriptions are present tense, 1-3 sentences, about the place, not the characters.
DESCRIPTION RULE: a description says only what the place IS now. Visible physical traces of the past are fine, because they are there now ("scorch marks blacken the beams", "an old brass rail shows under the gold leaf"). Never narrate the change itself: no "has been replaced by", "was transformed", "was once", "now". History goes in notes instead: a short append_notes on the place's area, e.g. {"op":"append_notes","area":"riverton:drowned_rat","text":"Formerly the Drowned Rat inn; transmogrified into a palace by magic."}. Exception: a temporary change with "lasts" (smoke, a fresh fire) may mention the event.
People and creatures mentioned in a room's description or notes are part of the room: if the story permanently changed one (hurt, killed, transformed, left, moved in), rewrite that part, following the description rule.

prompts.title: Map changes: which places (system prompt)
prompts.description: Step 1 of 2: the system prompt for 'which places changed'. First of the two calls that turn a flagged story change into a map change. {{reply}} is the shared base line pick.base_json.
prompts.locked: The game reads the JSON answer.
prompts.text: You read a short piece of a role-play story and a list of places on a map. You decide which places the story really changed on the map, for good or for a while (burned, collapsed, flooded, filled with smoke, doors smashed or barricaded, walls knocked through, rooms destroyed, a portal or passage opened for an hour). Moment-to-moment action that leaves no trace (walking, talking, fighting, a door simply opened and shut) is not a map change. {{reply}}.

prompts.title: Narration: how to report a person (tags)
prompts.description: Piece: fills {{how_to_report}} when map tools are off.
prompts.locked: The game reads these [ws_npc: …] tags.
prompts.text: If you invent a new fact about someone listed above (a scar, a kin's name, a favor), end your reply with [ws_npc: fact | their-id | the fact]. A memory highlight is [ws_npc: memory | their-id | the note]. If they leave the scene, [ws_npc: leave | their-id]. If they stay past the time they are due, [ws_npc: staying | their-id]. If they come along, [ws_npc: follow | their-id]. If they stop coming along, [ws_npc: stay | their-id]. Do not use a saved person as an unnamed stranger.

Call it with action "detail" only when you would otherwise invent something important about them. Do not use a saved person as an unnamed stranger.

For fact, memory and detail, put the text in text. For disposition, value is hostile, unfriendly, indifferent, friendly or helpful, and reason is why. Use detail only when you would otherwise invent something important.
